packs.definition: AI that answers, routes, or assists resident phone and chat contact: virtual agents and IVR bots, voice AI, agent-assist and after-call summarization, and the cloud contact-center (CCaaS) platforms they run on. This pack does not cover website-only chatbots with no contact-center function (see the public-comms pack) or anything that determines eligibility or flags fraud from a call (that adds the eligibility-case-mgmt overlay).

diligence_questions.good_answer: A written formula with numerator and denominator, exclusions named, and the same metric reported for named government clients at both time points.
diligence_questions.question: Show the exact formula for the containment or resolution rate you quoted. Do abandons, IVR completions, transfers, or 7-day callbacks count? Give the same metric for your three most comparable government clients at 90 days and 12 months.
diligence_questions.red_flag: A single marketing number with no formula, or a definition that counts abandons and menu completions as contained.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Three named agencies with contact information, and metrics that match the deck's claims.
diligence_questions.question: Name three government agencies of comparable volume and program type in production today, with contacts who will confirm your deck's metrics.
diligence_questions.red_flag: Refusal is disqualifying. Every credible vendor in this category has named references; "our customer list is confidential" is not an acceptable answer here.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Immediate escalation on request, automatic escalation after failures, a clear after-hours path, and warm transfer with full context.
diligence_questions.question: Walk us through every path to a human: what happens when a caller says "agent" on turn one? After two failed answers? At 2 a.m.? Is the transfer warm, meaning the agent sees the transcript and the collected data?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Escalation requires fighting through the bot, has no after-hours path, or drops the caller's context at transfer.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Corpus-restricted generation with per-answer citations, explicit refusal or escalation when the answer is absent, a measured wrong-answer rate with methodology, and yes to a pre-award test.
diligence_questions.question: Is the system restricted to content we approve, with the source cited for each answer? What does it do when the answer is not there: guess, refuse, or escalate? What is the measured wrong-answer rate on a benefits test set, and can we run our own test before award?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Open-ended generation, no citations, no measured wrong-answer rate, or resistance to pre-award testing.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Specific contract language on correction timelines and indemnification for bot-caused harm.
diligence_questions.question: If the bot gives a claimant wrong information, what does the contract say? What are the correction SLAs and the indemnification terms?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "That has never happened" or a disclaimer-only answer. A tribunal held Air Canada liable for its bot's invented policy; the agency owns what its bot says.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named language list matched to caller demographics, native-speaker QA, and a working interpreter handoff.
diligence_questions.question: Which languages do you support, on which channels, with what human review? Is spoken Spanish actual Spanish reviewed by native speakers? Show us the interpreter-handoff flow.
diligence_questions.red_flag: A large language count with no QA process. Washington state removed an AI voice in February 2026 after Spanish callers got Spanish-accented English.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named client on the same stack, fixed-price integration, and a precise read/write scope.
diligence_questions.question: Have you integrated with our exact stack (our IVR plus our CRM or eligibility system)? Name the client. Is the integration fixed-price? What does the bot read, and what does it write?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Our API can integrate with anything" with no named client on your stack, or open-ended integration billing.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A product-level authorization you can verify on the marketplace, a named storage location and retention period, and a written no-training commitment.
diligence_questions.question: Which FedRAMP or GovRAMP authorization does this specific product hold? Where are recordings and transcripts stored, how long are they retained, and is any of our data used to train models, yours or a subprocessor's?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Compliant" instead of "authorized," company-level claims for a product-level question, or vague data-use terms.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Named model providers and hosting, plus a described regression-test process tied to model updates.
diligence_questions.question: Which LLM and speech-recognition vendors are under the hood, and where are they hosted? When the underlying model updates, how do you regression-test our flows before residents see the change?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Refusal to name subprocessors, or no regression-testing process at all.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Disclosure on by default, prior-express-consent handling for outbound calls, and specific answers on state laws.
diligence_questions.question: Does the system disclose that it is automated at the start of each interaction? For outbound calls: how do you comply with FCC ruling 24-17, which treats AI voices as artificial voices under the TCPA? How do you handle state bot-disclosure laws and the Colorado AI Act (effective Jun 30, 2026)?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Disclosure treated as optional or configurable off, or unfamiliarity with FCC 24-17.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A line-item decomposition with surge modeling and stated minimums.
diligence_questions.question: Break the price into platform, per-minute or per-message usage, telecom passthrough, AI metering, integration, and support. What happens to our bill in a 10x claims surge? What are the minimums and the overage rates?
diligence_questions.red_flag: One bundled number, no surge answer, or minimums that only appear in the contract draft.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Full transcript access, per-intent reporting, staff review rights, and a no-cost or low-cost export commitment in a usable format.
diligence_questions.question: Do we get raw transcripts plus a dashboard covering containment, escalation, abandonment, wait time, and per-intent accuracy? Can our staff review any interaction? What is exported at contract end, in what format, and at what cost?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Vendor-controlled reporting only, sampled transcripts, or export treated as a paid professional service.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Automatic failover to the human queue, a specific uptime SLA, and real postmortems shared.
diligence_questions.question: When your AI is down, what does a caller hear: a queue or a dead line? What is your uptime SLA, and can we see your last two incident postmortems?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No failover story, or refusal to share incident history.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Yes, agent-assist can be bought alone (the lowest-risk entry point), with a described human review step for summaries that become records.
diligence_questions.question: Can we buy after-call summarization alone, without a resident-facing bot? What accuracy review exists for auto-summaries written into our CRM?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Bundling that forces a resident-facing bot, or summaries written to the CRM with no review.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named client, with before-and-after quality metrics alongside the staffing change.
diligence_questions.question: If you project staffing savings, name the client where that happened and tell us what happened to their quality metrics afterward.
diligence_questions.red_flag: Projected savings with no named client. Klarna reversed its agent-replacement strategy after quality suffered.

failure_modes.description: A bot on an official government line invents policy and residents rely on it. The organization owns everything its bot says: a Canadian tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's invented refund policy (https://www.cbsnews.com/news/aircanada-chatbot-discount-customer/), and even Cursor, an AI company, saw its own support bot invent a policy that did not exist (Ars Technica, Apr 17, 2025).
failure_modes.named_incident: NYC's MyCity chatbot told businesses to break the law (The Markup, Mar 29, 2024)
failure_modes.title: Hallucinated benefit or legal guidance on an official line

failure_modes.description: Klarna publicly reversed its "AI replaced 700 agents" posture and rehired humans (Forbes, May 18, 2025; direct article URL pending re-capture, see known gaps). For callers in crisis, callers with limited English, and callers with low digital literacy, a bot with no exit to a person is a due-process problem. The IRS voice-bot rollout is the design benchmark: taxpayers can always reach an English- or Spanish-speaking representative.
failure_modes.named_incident: Klarna reversed its AI-only support strategy and rehired human agents (Forbes, May 18, 2025)
failure_modes.title: Missing or buried human escalation

failure_modes.description: Vendors count abandons, IVR menu completions, and "caller did not reply" as "contained." Gartner's own bullish forecast is 80% of common issues resolved without a human by 2029 (https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-03-05-gartner-predicts-agentic-ai-will-autonomously-resolve-80-percent-of-common-customer-service-issues-without-human-intervention-by-2029), so a higher present-tense claim deserves the metric-definition question below.
failure_modes.named_incident: Documented government reality: Tamarac, FL reached 20% full self-service, and West Virginia's roughly 90% came from a narrow scripted FAQ surge line
failure_modes.title: Containment inflation through definition games

failure_modes.description: Intercom's $0.99 "outcome" pricing includes a customer who simply goes silent. Gartner predicts generative-AI cost-per-resolution will exceed offshore human cost by 2030 (Gartner press release, Jan 26, 2026), and pricing-model churn (Salesforce, Jun 2026; HubSpot, Apr 2026) makes a multi-year per-resolution commitment unsafe without a contractual resolution definition and an audit right.
failure_modes.named_incident: Intercom's published per-resolution pricing counts a customer who goes silent as a resolved outcome
failure_modes.title: Per-resolution pricing games

failure_modes.description: Washington state removed an AI voice after Spanish-speaking callers got Spanish-accented English instead of Spanish (StateScoop, Feb 27, 2026; direct article URL pending re-capture, see known gaps). The contrast benchmark is Minnesota's community-informed four-language model, with languages chosen from caller demographics.
failure_modes.named_incident: Washington state removed an AI voice over failed Spanish support (StateScoop, Feb 27, 2026)
failure_modes.title: Language-access failures shipped without native-speaker QA

failure_modes.description: FCC ruling 24-17 classifies AI-generated voices as "artificial" under the TCPA, so outbound use requires prior express consent. The FBI has warned about cloning of official voices (NPR, Jul 9, 2025). A synthetic voice marketed as indistinguishable from a human is a liability, not a feature.
failure_modes.named_incident: FCC declaratory ruling 24-17 on AI voices under the TCPA (Feb 2024)
failure_modes.title: Voice cloning and disclosure exposure

inclusion_test: Does the pitch mention phone calls, IVR, voice agents, hold times, call deflection or containment, or contact-center agents?
Does it target 311, benefits hotlines, unemployment lines, DMV lines, or "resident support"?
Does it offer agent-assist, call summarization, or transcription for call-center staff?
Does it name a CCaaS platform (Amazon Connect, Genesys, NICE, Five9, Talkdesk) as its base?
packs.incumbent_landscape: Three layers, and the first triage step is establishing which layer the sender occupies. Layer 1, platforms: AWS (Amazon Connect), Google Cloud (Customer Engagement Suite, formerly "Contact Center AI"), Genesys, NICE, Five9, Talkdesk, Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow, and Verint/SoundHound, all with real, named state and local deployments. Layer 2, the integrators and BPOs who deliver most state deployments: Deloitte (TrueServe on AWS), Accenture (Texas TWC "Larry"), Quantiphi/Presidio/Cisco (Illinois IDES), Smartronix (West Virginia), C1 Gov (NYC DSS), and Maximus. When a platform pitches, ask who delivers. When an integrator pitches, ask which platform. The accountability split between the two is where deployments fail. Layer 3, startups: govtech-native companies (Polimorphic, Citibot) with named local-government customers, versus commercial AI-agent startups (Sierra, Decagon, Parloa, PolyAI, Replicant). We could not verify any U.S. state or local government customer for that second group in public sources as of August 2026, so a "government-proven" claim from that cohort is unverified until the vendor names an agency you can call.

packs.legal_context:
- FCC declaratory ruling 24-17 (Feb 2024): AI-generated voices are
  "artificial voices" under the TCPA; outbound use requires prior express
  consent (https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-24-17A1.pdf).
- California B.O.T. Act (SB 1001, effective 2019): bots that try to
  influence a purchase or a vote must disclose that they are bots.
- Utah AI Policy Act (2024): disclosure requirements for generative AI in
  consumer interactions.
- Colorado AI Act (effective Jun 30, 2026): AI affecting access to
  government services is treated as high-risk. Verify current status before
  citing; the effective date has shifted once already.
- Executive Order 14224 (2025) does not erase Title VI language-access
  obligations. A vendor citing it as a reason to cut language QA is a red
  flag. Enforcement posture after the EO is unsettled; treat as uncertain.
packs.realistic_pricing:
Per-seat CCaaS list prices: Genesys $75–240 per user per month
(https://www.genesys.com/pricing), Five9 from $119–159 with a 50-seat
minimum, Talkdesk $85–225. Consumption pricing: Amazon Connect $0.038 per
voice minute and $0.010 per chat message
(https://aws.amazon.com/connect/pricing/). Rule of thumb: at roughly
$0.04–0.10 per minute all-in, a 500,000-call-per-year line at 5 minutes per
call runs about $100K–250K per year in platform consumption before
integration and telecom. A quote at 10x that level means asking which layer
the money is in. Per-resolution pricing is workable for digital FAQ traffic
only, and only with a contractual definition of "resolution." Govtech
startups typically sell annual jurisdiction-tier subscriptions, commonly low
five figures for small jurisdictions; that figure is uncertain, so negotiate
per jurisdiction.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: A containment or deflection rate of 80% or more (for voice, 40% or more)
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Text containment at or above 80%; voice containment at or above 40–50%
skepticism_triggers.why: Gartner's optimistic forecast is 80% of common issues by 2029. Documented government reality: Tamarac reached 20% full self-service, and West Virginia's roughly 90% came from a narrow scripted FAQ surge line.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "99%+ accuracy" or "never hallucinates"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any accuracy claim without a test-set methodology
skepticism_triggers.why: NYC and Cursor show that well-resourced deployers still ship wrong-answer bots. An accuracy number with no test set, denominator, or judge is a marketing number.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Replaces N agents" or a named dollar-savings figure
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any named FTE or dollar savings without an audited source
skepticism_triggers.why: Illinois's "$100M per year savings" was an initial vendor-story estimate, not an audited figure, and Klarna reversed its agent-replacement strategy.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Deploy in days" combined with "integrated"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: A deployment promise under 30 days alongside claims of system integration
skepticism_triggers.why: The two claims contradict each other. Days is true only for scripted FAQ bots (Texas TWC's "Larry": 5 days; West Virginia: 72 hours, both 2020 surge lines). Claim-status or eligibility integration takes months.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: Per-resolution price under $1, or an undefined "resolution"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Under $1 per resolution, or no contractual definition
skepticism_triggers.why: Intercom's $0.99 outcome pricing counts a customer who goes silent. Demand a contractual resolution definition plus an audit right.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "FedRAMP compliant" or "StateRAMP compliant"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: The word "compliant" instead of "authorized"
skepticism_triggers.why: "Compliant" is not "authorized." Verify the specific product at the FedRAMP Marketplace and on the GovRAMP authorized product list. A vendor still saying "StateRAMP" does not know the program became GovRAMP in February 2025.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Supports 75+ languages"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: A language count above the number of languages with native-speaker QA
skepticism_triggers.why: Machine-translation coverage is not language access. Ask which languages have native-speaker QA. Minnesota's four-language community-informed model is the honest benchmark.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "No integration required"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any claim that useful answers need no system integration
skepticism_triggers.why: It means FAQ-only. The bot cannot answer "where is my payment," which is most benefits-line volume.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Indistinguishable from a human voice"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any pitch marketing voice realism without disclosure
skepticism_triggers.why: FCC 24-17 treats AI voices as artificial under the TCPA, several states require bot disclosure, and the Colorado AI Act takes effect Jun 30, 2026. Realism without disclosure is a liability.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Government-proven" with no named agency
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Zero named, callable government customers
skepticism_triggers.why: This applies with force to commercial AI-agent startups (the Sierra, Decagon, Parloa, PolyAI, Replicant cohort). We could not verify any U.S. state or local government customer for that cohort in public sources as of August 2026.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: A new platform pitched as the fix for a struggling program
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Replatforming presented as the remedy for backlogs, improper payments, or debt problems
skepticism_triggers.why: California's billion-dollar EDDNext replatforming had not resolved the underlying fraud and debt problems (KQED, Dec 4, 2024; direct article URL pending re-capture, see known gaps). Process problems follow the program onto the new platform.

packs.definition: AI and analytics that inform government decisions: dashboards and BI with AI layers, "ask your data" LLM interfaces, predictive analytics, risk scoring, fraud and program-integrity analytics, and assessment algorithms. The first question in this pack is the fork: decoration or decision? A dashboard that describes gets standard scrutiny. A score or flag that can trigger action against a person is an adverse-action system and adds the eligibility-case-mgmt overlay.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A clear scope statement. If adverse actions are possible, the vendor accepts the high-impact review track without argument.
diligence_questions.question: What decisions will these outputs feed, and can a score or flag by itself trigger an adverse action against a person (a benefit cut, a fraud hold, an investigation)? If yes, we will treat this as a high-impact system that needs a different review track.
diligence_questions.red_flag: "That depends on how you configure it," without engaging the consequences.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Real notice text with specific reasons a caseworker can explain.
diligence_questions.question: Show the exact notice text an affected resident would receive. Can a caseworker explain in plain language why this specific person was flagged?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No notice exists because "the score is advisory."

diligence_questions.good_answer: Yes, in contract. Idaho's K.W. v. Armstrong shows trade-secret postures fail in court.
diligence_questions.question: Will you contractually commit to disclosing model logic, features, and weights to us, our auditors, and a court if litigated?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Trade-secret carve-outs over decision logic.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Threshold-level precision and recall plus a staffing model. The IRS benchmark shows 81% false positives is what "working" can look like at low base rates.
diligence_questions.question: Not "accuracy": what are precision and recall at your recommended threshold, validated on data like ours? At our prevalence, how many flags per 100 are false positives, and what staffing does the review queue require?
diligence_questions.red_flag: A single accuracy number.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Human sign-off enforced in the system design, not just in policy.
diligence_questions.question: Where exactly is human review mandatory, as a designed control? Can the system technically execute an adverse action with no human sign-off?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Auto-execution is possible and "most customers add review."

diligence_questions.good_answer: Shared testing results and a straight answer on regulatory attention.
diligence_questions.question: What testing across race, disability, age, and language has been done, on which population, and will you share the results? Has any customer, regulator, or DOJ inquiry examined this product?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Bias-free" claims, or evasion about known inquiries.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Explicit data-quality gates and uncertainty flags.
diligence_questions.question: When our input data is wrong, stale, or missing, does the system flag uncertainty or silently score anyway?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Silent scoring. Idaho scored unreliable data; Missouri's algorithm shipped with syntax errors.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A monitoring regime with named owners and suspension triggers.
diligence_questions.question: What drift monitoring and revalidation exist, who sees the results, and what triggers suspension of the model?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No revalidation after go-live.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A defect-to-remediation workflow that can enumerate all affected people.
diligence_questions.question: When we discover a wrong score, what is the process to correct it, find everyone else affected by the same defect, and make them whole?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Correction handled case by case with no systematic lookback.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Full provenance: every claim links to the query and rows behind it.
diligence_questions.question: For LLM insight layers: how do you prevent hallucinated numbers, and does every generated claim link to the underlying query and rows?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Generated narratives with no provenance.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A complete list including the hard cases. This tool cross-checks vendor names against the BTAH case library and the AI Incident Database.
diligence_questions.question: List the government deployments of this specific model or product, including any that were challenged, audited, or decommissioned.
diligence_questions.red_flag: Logos-only marketing, or omission of documented challenges.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Concrete terms sized to the documented downside (Michigan: $20M plus a rebuild; Florida: a $92.4M rebuild).
diligence_questions.question: What warranty, indemnification, and insurance terms apply when system errors trigger litigation?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Liability capped at fees paid.

packs.legal_context:
- The due-process line of cases, Goldberg v. Kelly (1970) through K.W. v.
  Armstrong (D. Idaho; 2025 contempt finding): scores that affect people
  must be explainable and contestable
  (https://www.acluidaho.org/en/cases/kw-v-armstrong).
- State v. Loomis (Wis. 2016): judicial caution on trade-secret risk
  scores in consequential decisions
  (https://harvardlawreview.org/print/vol-130/state-v-loomis/).
- OMB M-25-21 (2025): fraud detection is presumptively high-impact AI,
  with required testing, human oversight, and appeals.
- State automated-decision-system laws: New York's LOADinG Act
  (meaningful human review) and California SIMM 150 risk ratings for
  decision systems.
packs.realistic_pricing:

BI (Power BI, Tableau) is commodity-priced per seat and often already
licensed. Treat pricing as secondary to the decoration-or-decision fork:
until questions q01 through q05 have good answers, the price of an
adverse-action scoring system is not the issue.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A field-level number with methodology, and an unhesitating yes to a pilot on your real document mix.
diligence_questions.question: What field-level accuracy do you achieve on documents like ours, and will you demonstrate it in a pilot on 250–1,000 of our real documents, including faxes, phone photos, and handwriting?
diligence_questions.red_flag: One blended "99%" figure, or benchmark scores from public datasets instead of your documents.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A precise definition. 99% character accuracy can mean roughly 80% field accuracy and far lower document-level accuracy.
diligence_questions.question: Is that character, field, or document accuracy? Define the denominator.
diligence_questions.red_flag: The vendor cannot or will not say what the denominator is.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Production numbers in the 65–84% range with a clear definition. Covered California reports 84%; California DMV reports 65–70%.
diligence_questions.question: What straight-through-processing rate do your government customers achieve in production, and how do you define STP?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Claims above 90% before any pilot on your documents.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A concrete routing design, a staffing model, and a cost estimate at your volume.
diligence_questions.question: Show the human review workflow: how do confidence scores route low-confidence fields, who staffs the queue, and what does that labor cost at our volume?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "No human review needed." Mature agencies mandate review at any accuracy level.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A direct number backed by calibration data. Ten or fewer is consistent with the stated confidence.
diligence_questions.question: If we sample 100 fields you marked at 90% confidence or higher, how many will be wrong?
diligence_questions.red_flag: More than 10 wrong signals miscalibrated confidence scores; no answer signals it has never been measured.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A line-item price at your volume with a written definition of a page.
diligence_questions.question: What is the all-in price per 1,000 pages at our real volume: API or license fees, feature add-ons, review tooling, integration, and reprocessing? And what counts as a "page"?
diligence_questions.red_flag: A single per-page teaser rate. Full extraction runs 20–47x plain OCR once features stack.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Written terms. Anchors: Azure deletes in 24 hours and does not train; Google does not train; AWS requires an explicit organization-level opt-out.
diligence_questions.question: Where is our data processed and stored, is it used to train your models or any third party's, and what is the deletion timeline? We need this in writing.
diligence_questions.red_flag: Verbal assurances, or terms that defer to an upstream provider's defaults.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Named engines and a subprocessor list. This separates platforms from wrappers.
diligence_questions.question: Which underlying OCR or extraction engine or foundation model do you use, and which subprocessors touch our documents?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Proprietary" used as a reason not to name the engines the pitch depends on.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Product-level authorizations you can verify yourself on the FedRAMP Marketplace and the GovRAMP list.
diligence_questions.question: Which authorizations do you hold: FedRAMP (at what level), GovRAMP, SOC 2 Type II? Can you support IRS Pub 1075, HIPAA, or SNAP confidentiality requirements as applicable?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Compliant" language, a SOC 2 Type I passed off as Type II, or authorizations that exist only company-wide.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Both numbers reported separately, plus a described QA step on the residual.
diligence_questions.question: For redaction: give us precision and recall separately. What percentage of PII do you miss, and what QA catches misses before records go public?
diligence_questions.red_flag: One blended "success rate." A missed SSN is a disclosure incident.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Named references. SSA, VA, Colorado HCPF, Missouri DSS, California DMV, Covered California, King County, and the Arkansas courts all exist in this category.
diligence_questions.question: Name three government references at agencies our size, in production 12 or more months, including one where the rollout was hard.
diligence_questions.red_flag: "References are confidential."

diligence_questions.good_answer: A complete exportable audit trail and a drift-monitoring process.
diligence_questions.question: What per-document audit trail exists (model version, confidence score, every human touch), exportable for QC and inspector-general staff? What happens when document formats drift?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No per-document trail. GAO names opacity as the accountability risk in this category (GAO-26-109137).

diligence_questions.good_answer: A written export commitment with format and cost.
diligence_questions.question: What are the exit terms: can we export our trained models, templates, and labeled data at contract end, and at what cost?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Export treated as a change order, or trained artifacts owned by the vendor.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named language list with measured quality per language.
diligence_questions.question: Which languages do you support, as a named list matched to our limited-English-proficiency population, not an adjective?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Multilingual" with no list and no measurements.

failure_modes.title: Benchmark-to-production accuracy gap

failure_modes.description: At an honest 80% STP rate on 1 million pages per year, the 200,000 exception pages equal roughly three or more FTEs of review labor, plus per-review tooling fees (AWS A2I lists $0.03 per reviewed page, https://aws.amazon.com/augmented-ai/pricing/). failure_modes.description: Provider defaults differ sharply. AWS allows service-improvement use of content unless the organization opts out (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_ai-opt-out.html), Azure deletes inputs within 24 hours (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/responsible-ai/document-intelligence/data-privacy-security), and Google does not train on customer content (https://docs.cloud.google.com/document-ai/docs/data-usage). A startup wrapper calling a commercial LLM adds an unvetted second processor. Benefits documents implicate IRS Pub 1075, HIPAA, and SNAP confidentiality rules.

packs.incumbent_landscape: A mature category being disrupted by LLM-native extraction. Gartner's first IDP Magic Quadrant (Sep 3, 2025) covers a market of 100+ vendors with five Leaders: ABBYY, Hyperscience, Infrrd, Tungsten Automation, and UiPath (https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/6912666). Five tiers: (1) hyperscaler APIs (AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, Google Document AI), usually arriving inside an integrator's pitch; (2) enterprise IDP platforms (the Leaders above, plus WorkFusion, IBM Datacap, OpenText Captiva, Grooper); (3) government redaction specialists (Extract Systems, CSI Intellidact); (4) ECM incumbents with AI add-ons (Laserfiche, Hyland OnBase, Tyler). Check whether your existing ECM contract already includes capture or IDP before engaging a new vendor; many cold pitches duplicate capability you already own. (5) LLM-native startups (Extend, Reducto, Sensible, Instabase, LandingAI, Nanonets, Docsumo). Most inbound cold email comes from this tier, and few of these hold FedRAMP or GovRAMP authorizations or named U.S. state references. The core triage insight: many pitches are thin wrappers over the same three hyperscaler APIs. Ask what engine is actually under the hood.

packs.legal_context:
- IRS Publication 1075 (federal tax information safeguards) applies when
  processed documents contain FTI. Standing requirement as of Aug 28, 2026.
- HIPAA applies to health documents; a business associate agreement is
  required.
- SNAP confidentiality rules (7 CFR 272.1) restrict use and disclosure of
  applicant information.
- State breach-notification laws apply to processing failures that expose
  PII.
- Title VI language-access obligations extend to how documents from
  limited-English-proficiency residents are handled.

A 1-million-page-per-year program at full-feature Textract rates is roughly

packs.definition: AI that touches who gets benefits or what happens to their case: eligibility screening and determination, renewals, verification, fraud detection and identity-proofing, case-management copilots, benefit-notice generation, and work-requirement compliance tooling. This is the only pack where a software error is, by legal definition, a deprivation of a constitutionally protected property interest (Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254). Not this pack alone: pure document extraction (see document-processing, unless the output feeds determinations) and applicant-side benefit screeners that only widen access, which sit in a different risk class.

diligence_questions.good_answer: An unambiguous "a named human makes every adverse decision," with UI evidence showing how.
diligence_questions.question: Does your system ever deny, reduce, terminate, or flag-for-fraud on its own, or does a named human make every adverse decision?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Configurable," "auto-adjudication," or any hedging. This question has no acceptable middle answer.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Actual notice text that satisfies 42 CFR 431.210 (Medicaid) or 7 CFR 273.13 (SNAP): specific reasons, specific regulation.
diligence_questions.question: Show the exact notice a person receives after an AI-influenced denial. Does it state the specific factual reasons and the regulation relied on?
diligence_questions.red_flag: A generic template, or a generated paragraph offered as the "explanation."

diligence_questions.good_answer: Yes to both, in writing. Idaho's K.W. v. Armstrong establishes that due process outranks trade secrets.
diligence_questions.question: On appeal, can you produce the complete record (inputs, extractions, model version, what the human saw and did), and will you commit in contract that nothing is withheld as a trade secret?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Any trade-secret carve-out over decision logic.

diligence_questions.good_answer: State-specific evaluation results with a defined denominator, or an honest "we have not measured that yet."
diligence_questions.question: What is your measured accuracy on OUR state's rules, evaluated against our policy manual and historically adjudicated cases, and what is the denominator?
diligence_questions.red_flag: A generic accuracy number from another state or from a demo corpus.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Published or shareable breakouts, plus support for independent testing.
diligence_questions.question: Break error rates out by language, disability status, age, and, where lawful, race and ethnicity. What disparate-performance testing exists, and will you support our own pre-deployment and annual testing?
diligence_questions.red_flag: "Our AI is unbiased" with no data behind it.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A confidence-threshold design, the share of items routed to humans, and sampling audits of high-confidence outputs.
diligence_questions.question: What happens when the model is wrong but confident?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No sampling of high-confidence outputs; those are exactly the errors that reach residents.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named process with a turnaround commitment and regression testing.
diligence_questions.question: Who updates the system when our state plan, waivers, or verification rules change, how fast, and how is the change tested?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No update pipeline. NYC's chatbot stayed wrong for roughly two years.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Written no-training terms and authorizations you can verify at https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/ and https://govramp.org/. "In process" is not "authorized."
diligence_questions.question: Where does our data go? Is applicant data used to train models or shared with third parties? Which of these do you hold: GovRAMP or FedRAMP authorization, SOC 2 Type II, IRS Pub 1075 and HIPAA compliance?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Verbal assurances, or "compliant" phrasing.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A knowledgeable answer about 45 CFR 95.611 and named states where the vendor navigated it.
diligence_questions.question: Does this require an APD amendment or CMS/FNS sign-off, and have you been through that process in other states?
diligence_questions.red_flag: A vendor who has never heard of an APD has never really deployed in this space.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Named production references plus any independent evaluation. Cross-check the CCF AI Knowledge Hub and Code for America's landscape assessment.
diligence_questions.question: Name three comparable agencies in production, not pilots, that we can call. What independent evaluations of your product exist?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Pilots presented as production, or logos with no callable contact.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Real numbers: a plausible per-item review time and a nonzero override rate.
diligence_questions.question: What is the caseworker's realistic review burden: items per worker per day, and your own override-rate data?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No override data, or volumes that make real review impossible. Near-zero overrides means rubber-stamping.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A concrete plan: affected-case query capability, notification templates, a reinstatement workflow, and timelines.
diligence_questions.question: What is your rollback plan? If we find a systematic error, how fast can we identify every affected case, notify people, and reinstate benefits?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No answer here means no deployment.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Contractual acceptance of indemnification and audit rights.
diligence_questions.question: Who bears liability for wrongful denials caused by system error, and will you accept indemnification and audit-rights clauses?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Liability pushed entirely onto the agency. Deloitte's "not our systems" posture shows why this must be contractual.

packs.incumbent_landscape: Integrators and COTS: Deloitte dominates integrated eligibility (25+ states, $5B+ in contracts, roughly 53 million Medicaid enrollees on its systems, per KFF Health News: https://kffhealthnews.org/news/article/medicaid-deloitte-run-eligibility-systems-plagued-by-errors/). Accenture, Gainwell, Conduent, and Optum populate the Medicaid systems ecosystem; Maximus is the dominant eligibility-support BPO now marketing AI; Merative Curam (formerly IBM) is the social-program COTS; Salesforce and ServiceNow push case-management-on-platform; RedMane, Diona, and Northwoods sell human-services-specific tooling. Critical context: the incumbents' deterministic systems, before any generative AI, produced wrong notices, impossible deadlines, 25,000 erroneous Kentucky terminations, and 2026 Michigan disability miscoverage (https://www.npr.org/2026/07/20/nx-s1-5896359/medicaid-disabled-patients-denied-deloitte-michigan). Deloitte's defense ("they're not Deloitte systems") shows accountability allocation is contested even among the biggest incumbents, so a listing in this pack is emphatically not a safety signal. The legitimate near-term AI layer is document and intake automation (Hyperscience in Colorado and Missouri; Pennsylvania legibility scanning; New Jersey document validation; North Carolina summarization, per Code for America: https://codeforamerica.org/explore/government-ai-landscape-assessment/). The 2025–26 copilot wave: Nava PBC (the most methodologically transparent, with an open-source Caseworker Empowerment Toolkit and published guardrails), the Maryland and Anthropic navigation agent, Augintel, and frontier-lab GSA OneGov seats putting near-free LLMs inside agencies. AI increasingly arrives through staff tooling, not procurement. The highest-risk adjacent lane is fraud and identity vendors (SAS and FAST Enterprises in the MiDAS era; Pondera, now Thomson Reuters; LexisNexis; ID.me). Treat any "AI fraud detection" pitch as an adverse-action system, full stop.

packs.legal_context:
## Why this category is different

When AI touches who gets Medicaid, SNAP, unemployment, or child care
assistance, errors are not inconveniences. They are unlawful deprivations.
Courts have already ruled against automated benefits systems in Michigan
(a $20M settlement over false fraud accusations; auto-adjudicated fraud
findings wrong more than 90% of the time), Tennessee (due process and ADA
violations), and Arkansas and Idaho (invalidated care-cutting algorithms),
and Australia's Robodebt collapsed into a royal commission. Federal policy
(OMB M-25-21) presumes AI used in benefits adjudication and fraud
detection is "high-impact," requiring testing, human oversight, and
appeals, and several states now require meaningful human review by law.
This tool therefore applies its strictest evidence bar here: any vendor
claiming to automate or accelerate adverse decisions (denials, reductions,
terminations, fraud flags) is flagged for enhanced review regardless of
company size or references. AI that helps staff read documents, summarize
cases, and draft communications, with a named human making every decision,
appeal-ready explanations, and audit trails, can be evaluated on its
merits. AI that decides is not a product category this tool will ever mark
low-risk.

## Controlling law and policy

- Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970) and Mathews v. Eldridge (1976):
  the constitutional floor for process before benefits are taken away
  (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/397/254).
- 42 CFR 431.210 (Medicaid) and 7 CFR 273.13 (SNAP): what a legally
  sufficient adverse-action notice must contain.
- K.W. v. Armstrong (D. Idaho): no trade-secret shield over decision
  logic; 2025 contempt finding
  (https://www.acluidaho.org/en/cases/kw-v-armstrong).
- A.M.C. v. Smith (M.D. Tenn.): ADA liability attaches to
  eligibility-system failures
  (https://healthlaw.org/resource/case-explainer-amc-v-smith/).
- OMB M-25-21 (2025): benefits adjudication, continued-eligibility
  determination, and fraud detection are presumptively high-impact, with
  mandatory pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, monitoring, trained
  human oversight with a fail-safe, and remedies and appeals
  (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf).
- New York LOADinG Act: requires "continued, operational and meaningful
  human review." New York NYS-P24-001: "Automated final decision systems
  are not permitted."
- Texas TRAIGA (effective Jan 1, 2026). Verify current status before
  citing.
- Colorado AI Act (delayed to Jun 30, 2026). Verify current status before
  citing.
- 45 CFR 95.611: APD approval gates for changes to federally funded
  eligibility systems.
- California SIMM 150: rates "service eligibility assessments for housing
  or income assistance" at least Moderate risk.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Fully automated eligibility determination" or "touchless processing"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any such claim applied to adverse actions
skepticism_triggers.why: Presumptively disqualifying. This is the MiDAS and Robodebt pattern, and it maps to the tool's strongest caution band regardless of vendor pedigree.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Reduces fraud by X%"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any fraud-reduction percentage
skepticism_triggers.why: Demand the false-positive rate and what happens to flagged people while "under review." MiDAS was wrong more than 90% of the time.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "99%+ accuracy"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any accuracy claim without state-specific evaluation, a denominator, and breakouts by field, case type, language, and disability
skepticism_triggers.why: Blended accuracy hides exactly the errors that become wrongful denials.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Unbiased AI" or "bias-free AI"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any such claim
skepticism_triggers.why: Unfalsifiable. The honest form is "here is our disparate-performance testing and here are the results."

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Explainable AI" meaning a chatbot paragraph
skepticism_triggers.threshold: An explanation that is not a legally sufficient notice
skepticism_triggers.why: A generated paragraph is not a 42 CFR 431.210 notice. Ask to see actual notice text.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Proprietary; we cannot share how it works"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any trade-secret posture over decision logic
skepticism_triggers.why: K.W. v. Armstrong establishes that due process outranks trade secrets.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Deploy in weeks" for anything touching the eligibility system
skepticism_triggers.threshold: A deployment promise under 90 days
skepticism_triggers.why: It ignores APD and CMS/FNS approval gates (45 CFR 95.611). Kentucky's single defect took 10 months and $522K to fix.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Human in the loop" without numbers
skepticism_triggers.threshold: No items-per-reviewer-per-day or override-rate data
skepticism_triggers.why: Near-zero overrides means the human is a rubber stamp.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "FedRAMP compliant" or "StateRAMP compliant"; a SOC 2 Type I passed off as Type II
skepticism_triggers.threshold: The word "compliant" instead of "authorized"
skepticism_triggers.why: Verify authorization status on the marketplaces directly. "In process" is not "authorized."

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "Trusted by [state]"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: A reference that turns out to be an unpaid pilot or a constituent-services chatbot rebranded as eligibility tech
skepticism_triggers.why: Call the named agency and ask what is actually in production.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "AI will clear your backlog"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Backlog-clearing claims during unwinding or work-requirement crunches
skepticism_triggers.why: Speed pressure on adverse actions is precisely how Tennessee and Michigan happened.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: "We handle appeals too"
skepticism_triggers.threshold: The vendor adjudicating appeals of its own system's decisions
skepticism_triggers.why: A due-process conflict of interest.

skepticism_triggers.claim_pattern: Free pilots contingent on broad data access
skepticism_triggers.threshold: Any free pilot conditioned on access to applicant data
skepticism_triggers.why: A data-acquisition play. OMB M-25-21 tells federal agencies to bar vendor training on government data.

packs.incumbent_landscape: A crowded small-to-mid vendor field sells chatbots and AI search to cities and counties: K12 Insight, Apptegy, Element451, Citibot, Polimorphic, Tyler Technologies, and Verint, with documented contract pricing spanning roughly $5,600 basic to $759K+ enterprise (https://blogs.civiciq.com/2025/12/02/government-ai-chatbots-311-rfps-vendor-pricing-guide-2025/). Granicus is the communications incumbent: govDelivery claims a 300M+ subscriber network (vendor-reported) plus a "Government Experience Agent" (https://granicus.com/products/govdelivery/). State-portal chatbots have a decade of history: Mississippi "Missi" (Tyler, 2017), Georgia DOL "George A.I." (Cisco; 2.5 million+ users and an agency-claimed 97% accuracy we could not verify in public sources), Massachusetts "Ask MA" (NeuroSoph; roughly 1.2 million monthly users), Texas (Capgemini), Atlanta "Ava" (Zammo.ai), and Vermont "ChatVT," which gets annual performance reviews (https://statescoop.com/government-ai-chatbots-state-local-websites-2024/). For translation: Wordly for live meeting interpretation (Santa Barbara CA, North Las Vegas NV; https://www.wordly.ai/city-council-translation), and New Jersey DOL with U.S. Digital Response as the standout responsible machine-translation deployment (https://www.usdigitalresponse.org/resources/how-new-jersey-is-using-generative-ai-to-scale-their-human-centered-approach-to-language-access).

- The underlying technology stack of NYC's MyCity bot was not re-verified

diligence_questions.good_answer: A concrete, named differentiator and a defensible answer about the roadmap gap.
diligence_questions.question: We already license (or can nearly freely add) Microsoft 365 Copilot or Gemini. What specifically does your product do that they do not, and what happens to that gap when their next release ships?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Generic productivity claims that the bundled incumbent already covers.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Yes across all content types, in usable formats, demonstrated live.
diligence_questions.question: Can our records officers search, retrieve, export, and verifiably delete every prompt, output, transcript, and summary you hold, in a usable format, for a public-records request?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Export gaps for any content type, or export sold as a professional-services engagement.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Retention configurable to your schedules, with no uncontrollable content stores.
diligence_questions.question: Can retention be set to match our schedules, and is there any content (chat history, telemetry, backups) we cannot control?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Telemetry, chat history, or backups your records officers cannot control.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Written no-training terms, named data residency, and a deletion-at-exit commitment.
diligence_questions.question: Contractually: is our data used to train your models or any third party's? Where does it reside? What happens at contract end?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Silence on subprocessors, or "we may use data to improve services."

diligence_questions.good_answer: An affirmative-consent flow for every participant, including the public.
diligence_questions.question: How does the tool obtain affirmative consent from every participant, including non-users and the public, in all-party-consent states? What is your exposure to Otter.ai-style litigation?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Consent inferred from a bot being visible; that theory is being litigated in Brewer v. Otter.ai.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Technical blocklists for closed sessions and sensitive meeting types.
diligence_questions.question: Can we technically block the tool from closed sessions, attorney-client calls, HR meetings, and juvenile or health matters, or does it rely on staff remembering?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Reliance on staff remembering to turn it off.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Named authorization levels and the specific cloud tier; CJIS-touching work runs in GCC High or the equivalent.
diligence_questions.question: What FedRAMP level, GovRAMP status, and SOC 2 Type II do you hold, is the tool CJIS-compatible, and in which cloud does our tenant run?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Commercial cloud offered for CJIS or FTI workloads.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A measured error rate and UI that requires review before content becomes a record.
diligence_questions.question: What is the measured error rate for summaries and drafts, and what does the UI do to force human review (such as source-linking) before content becomes an official record?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No error measurement; summaries flowing into official records unreviewed.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Usage logs adequate for audit without keystroke-level surveillance.
diligence_questions.question: What usage logs do we get, and can we audit misuse without creating a workforce-surveillance problem?
diligence_questions.red_flag: Either no logs at all, or workforce surveillance by default.

diligence_questions.good_answer: Honest labeling of self-reported versus measured, with the methodology shared.
diligence_questions.question: Are your time-savings claims self-reported user estimates (like Pennsylvania's 95 minutes per day) or independently measured? Show the methodology.
diligence_questions.red_flag: Self-reported figures presented as measured savings.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A documented export process and certified deletion at termination.
diligence_questions.question: On termination, how do we get every record out, and how do you certify deletion?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No deletion certification.

diligence_questions.good_answer: A named customer that has been through it, and what they learned.
diligence_questions.question: Which government customers at our scale have completed a public-records request or a litigation hold involving your product's outputs? What broke?
diligence_questions.red_flag: No customer has ever tested the records path; you would be first.

packs.incumbent_landscape: This pack's defining fact: the incumbents are nearly free. Microsoft 365 Copilot reached GCC (Dec 2024) and GCC High (Dec 3, 2025), with a GSA OneGov deal giving Copilot at no added cost for up to 12 months with M365 G5 (https://www.nextgov.com/acquisition/2025/12/microsoft-makes-copilot-available-secure-cloud-customers/409912/). GSA's Gemini OneGov agreement priced the Google bundle at $0.47 per agency through Sep 30, 2026 (https://www.gsa.gov/about-gsa/newsroom/news-releases/gsa-google-announce-gemini-onegov-agreement-08212025), and similar roughly $1 offers exist for ChatGPT and Claude. It is uncertain whether state and local governments can ride OneGov terms (coverage is federal), but the pricing signal shapes the whole market. The best-documented state deployment is Pennsylvania's ChatGPT Enterprise pilot (175 employees, then 3,000+; roughly 95 minutes per day of self-reported time savings; https://digitalgovernmenthub.org/library/lessons-from-pennsylvanias-generative-ai-pilot-with-chatgpt/). Pennsylvania's approved-tool model (ChatGPT Enterprise and Copilot approved centrally, others case by case) is itself a useful triage pattern. Notetakers split between bundled defaults (Teams, Zoom, Meet) and standalones (Otter.ai, Fireflies, Rev, Verbit). The triage question for any startup in this pack: what does this do that the Copilot or Gemini the jurisdiction already (nearly) owns does not, at a price that beats near-zero?
packs.known_gaps:
- Whether state and local governments can use OneGov terms is uncertain;
  coverage is federal.
- No citable public-sector incident of copilot permission-sprawl
  oversharing was found in public sources; the risk is retained as a
  trigger with that caveat.
- The reported U.S. House Copilot restriction and California GenAI
  contract awards were excluded as unverified this cycle.
- The Gartner shadow-AI figure (69%) is a survey statistic reached
  through a secondary source.
packs.legal_context:
- State public-records law: Washington's archivist advice sheets (Jun
  2024) are the cleanest citable guidance that AI outputs, and likely
  prompts, are records
  (https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-02/advice-sheet-are-generative-ai-interactions-public-records-(june-2024).pdf).
- All-party-consent wiretap statutes (CA, FL, IL, MD, MA, MT, NV, NH, PA,
  WA) govern meeting recording by notetakers.
- Open-meetings acts govern recording and minutes of public bodies,
  including closed and executive sessions.
- New Jersey 25-OIT-001 (2025): sensitive PII only in state-approved AI
  tools
  (https://nj.gov/it/docs/ps/25-OIT-001-State-of-New-Jersey-Guidance-on-Responsible-Use-of-Generative-AI.pdf).
- Pennsylvania's ITP and New York NYS-G25-002 are the state AI-use policy
  models to check against.
- Cloud-tier compliance: CJIS, FTI (IRS Pub 1075), and HIPAA workloads
  must run in the matching government cloud tier (GCC or GCC High, or the
  equivalent). Commercial-cloud AI on those workloads is a compliance
  failure regardless of tool quality
  (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/requirements-licensing-gcc).
